records.name: Fiji
records.summary: Fiji is workable for trans visitors — the Pacific islands' leader. Same-sex relations decriminalised in 2010; the 2013 Constitution bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity AND expression — reportedly the only constitution in the world with that explicit pairing. Counterweights: no gender-marker change mechanism, and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network documents high rates of violence and harassment against trans people. Suva has an organised community (Haus of Khameleon, Rainbow Pride Foundation).

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct decriminalised 2010 (Crimes Act); Fiji among the first countries to ban SOGI discrimination constitutionally — SO protection in the 1997 Constitution, reinstated and expanded to gender identity and expression in the 2013 Constitution; workplace SO protections since 2007; health professionals barred from trying to change sexual orientation. Traditional third-gender vaka sa lewa lewa recognised culturally but no legal gender recognition route; no same-sex marriage/civil unions (Marriage Act 2002: one man, one woman); intersex bodily autonomy unprotected. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal per overview flag, LGR No, orgs cannot register.

Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Fiji' (2023): the 2013 Constitution's discrimination protection on gender identity and expression is described as unique worldwide, yet legislative/policy frameworks permit NO gender-marker change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities — headline constitutional protection with zero implementation for trans people, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.

Human Rights Watch (11 Apr 2005): two men (one an Australian tourist) received two-year prison sentences under colonial-era Penal Code Art 175 (up to 14 years) for consensual sex; HRW urged charges dropped and release, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on SO discrimination (Fiji one of first two countries worldwide, with South Africa); the judge called the acts 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Documents the enforcement era before the 2006 no-arrest policy and 2010 decriminalisation.

PinkNews (10 Jul 2006): the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex will no longer be arrested — the practical end of enforcement two years before the Crimes Act 2010 decriminalisation; NZ AIDS Foundation (Exec Dir Rachael Le Mesurier) linked criminalisation to undergrounding of sex and HIV spread.

GlobalGayz country page (pre-2013, undated): Fiji timeline — 1997 second country in the world to enshrine SO non-discrimination; 2006 no-arrest policy confirmed; 2007 state of emergency ousted PM; 2009 Constitution abolished; 1 Feb 2010 full decriminalisation under Crimes Act 2010; Marriage Act 2002 bars same-sex marriage; ~322-island archipelago. Legacy-era overview — its claim that SOGI discrimination was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution.

Sydney Morning Herald (14 Apr 2005): PM Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in 'the conservative Christian nation', days after an Australian tourist and a Fijian man received two-year sentences — the political/religious climate context behind the sodomy-law enforcement that HRW protested.

records.name: Samoa
records.summary:
Samoa is workable for trans visitors — anchored by one of the world's most institutionalized third-gender traditions. Fa'afafine (and fa'atama) are culturally embedded: recognized as heirs to customary land and eligible for matai (chiefly) titles within fa'a Sāmoa, organized nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association (a formal UN UPR stakeholder since 1987), and visible through a famous pageant culture. Samoa repealed its colonial-era “female impersonation” crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine (APTN peer-led study — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village fono councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.

sources.summary: APTN (9 May 2024): Nadi, Fiji convening gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua, PNG — documents the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum (fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga, fakafifine in Niue, etc.) as living community infrastructure Samoa participates in.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Samoa's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to 5 years under the Crimes Act 2013).

Samoa Fa'afafine Association (SFA) stakeholder report for Samoa's UPR (39th session, 2021): 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa' - describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Samoa's third gender (fa'afafine) delicately balancing sex and religion.
NOTE: The APTN Samoa socio-economic study returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

RNZ Pacific (3 May 2013): Samoa's new Crimes Act, in force that week, scrapped the crime of impersonating a woman — Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief; interview also confirms the community was not then agitating to repeal sodomy provisions, i.e. decriminalisation outcome on that front remained unchanged.

Schmidt, 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa' (Intersections, Aug 2001): fa'afafine = 'in the manner of a woman'; academic analysis argues fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality/transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone — background for how visitors may encounter the term.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fa'afafine of Samoa (with American Samoa and Tokelau) among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

records.name: Tuvalu
records.summary: Tuvalu demands real caution. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; very small, tight-knit, church-centred society; no specifically documented anti-trans violence (population ~11,000). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.summary: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Tuvalu: documents the legal status — male same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era provisions.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tuvalu: traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination including against women; no government abuses; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the Penal Code but no prosecutions.

Tuvalu Ministry of Health Global AIDS Progress Report 2017 (UNAIDS): the national HIV response, drawing on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations (including MSM and transgender Tuvaluans).

US Mission Geneva (22 Mar 2011): Tuvalu appears among roughly 80 signatory states of the UN joint statement recalling General Assembly resolutions on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity; also lists Asia-Pacific Forum and Council of Europe mechanisms used to press the issue. Documents Tuvalu's 2011 diplomatic position; dated but on-topic.

GlobalGayz Tuvalu archive: aggregates news and reports incl. an OHCHR Human Rights Day op-ed urging states to decriminalise consensual same-sex relations, plus historical items on Tuvalu's colonial-era sodomy-law status. Useful as a dated context and pointer source rather than primary authority.

records.name: Solomon Islands
records.summary: Solomon Islands is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years); no LGR; documented social hostility; weak state capacity post-Tensions; no open community infrastructure.

sources.summary: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Solomon Islands: documents the legal status — same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era law, up to 14 years.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: no security-force abuses; violence and discrimination against women prevalent; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the penal code but no prosecutions.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents lengthy pretrial detention, corruption, violence against women - general context; no LGBT-specific abuses reported.
US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents the RAMSI assistance mission, the Lusibaea case, and general human-rights conditions - baseline assessment.

SIBC (8 Jun 2018): Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that 'same sex marriage cannot populate the world' — a dated official statement of elite hostility to recognition; no same-sex marriage law exists and Parliament has not legislated one.

Human Dignity Trust profile: Solomon Islands criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, maximum penalty 14 years' imprisonment (Penal Code provisions); the profile documents the colonial-law basis and the absence of recorded prosecutions in recent years.

Wikipedia reference summary: male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal and punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, but the law is not enforced; LGBTQ people face legal challenges not experienced by other residents, with no relationship recognition or non-discrimination shield.
